blocks.content: Picture this. You walk into a system design interview and the interviewer says, design Twitter. That's it. No spec, no user stories, no list of features to build against. Just two words and a blank whiteboard.

Your first instinct might be to panic, or worse, to start drawing boxes right away. A database here, a load balancer there, a feed service somewhere in the middle. Stop. That instinct is exactly what this lesson exists to fix.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396383031-472985929.png
blocks.alt: A vague design prompt branching into several completely different valid interpretations

blocks.content: 1. Introduction

Every system design interview opens with some version of a vague prompt. Design Twitter, design Uber, design a URL shortener, design WhatsApp. None of these prompts come with a requirements document attached, and that is not an oversight on the interviewer's part. It is the whole point of the exercise.

This lesson covers the very first skill you need, before you draw a single box on the whiteboard: figuring out what you are actually being asked to build, and doing it out loud, in a way the interviewer can follow along with. Get this phase right and everything after it, the diagrams, the data model choices, the trade off discussions, gets noticeably easier, because you are now solving a problem you actually understand.
Get it wrong, and you can spend forty five minutes designing a beautifully scalable system that answers a question nobody actually asked.
2. Why a Vague Prompt Is Deliberate, Not a Trick
blocks.text: 2. Why a Vague Prompt Is Deliberate, Not a Trick

blocks.content: The first thing to internalize is that the vagueness is intentional. The interviewer is not being lazy, and they are not testing whether you can read their mind. They are testing something far more specific: can you take an open ended, real world sized problem and narrow it down into something you can actually design in the time you have.

Think about what an actual product like Twitter really is. It is a social graph, a feed ranking system, a search engine, a notifications pipeline, an ads platform, a trending topics service, a direct messaging product, and a dozen other systems stitched together over more than a decade. Nobody, in any interview, anywhere, is designing all of that on a whiteboard in forty five minutes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396383032-53026679.png
blocks.alt: Design Twitter branching into its real underlying subsystems: social graph, feed ranking, search, direct messages, and ads

blocks.content: So when the interviewer says design Twitter, what they actually mean is something closer to: show me how you turn design Twitter into something specific and buildable. The vagueness is the test. Your job is to remove it, out loud, by asking good questions.

blocks.title: This is a skill being graded, not a puzzle with one right answer
blocks.content: Interviewers usually don't have one secret correct scope hidden up their sleeve that you are supposed to guess. What they are grading is the process of narrowing down, not whether you happened to land on the exact scope they were picturing in their head.
3. Functional vs Non Functional Requirements

Once you start narrowing scope, you need a vocabulary for what you are actually narrowing. Every system design conversation splits requirements into two buckets, and mixing them up is one of the fastest ways to sound unprepared.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396383032-201027188.png
blocks.alt: Functional requirements like posting a tweet and following a user shown side by side with non functional requirements like low latency and high availability

blocks.content: 3.1 Functional Requirements
Functional requirements describe what the system actually does, the concrete actions a user can take. For a Twitter like product, that reads like a plain list of verbs.
["A user can post a tweet","A user can follow another user","A user can see a feed of tweets from people they follow","A user can like or reply to a tweet","A user can search for tweets or people"]
items: A user can post a tweet
A user can follow another user
A user can see a feed of tweets from people they follow
A user can like or reply to a tweet
A user can search for tweets or people

blocks.content: These are the easy ones to spot because you can literally point at a button in the app and say that. Most candidates naturally gravitate here first, and that is fine, but functional requirements alone don't tell you much about how hard the system actually is to build.
3.2 Non Functional Requirements

Non functional requirements describe the qualities the system needs to have while it does those things. They rarely show up as a button in the app, but they drive almost every real architectural decision you will make later in the interview.

["Latency, how fast a request needs to be served","Availability, how much downtime the system can tolerate","Consistency, whether every reader needs to see the same data at the same instant","Scale, how many users and requests the system needs to handle","Durability, whether data loss is acceptable under any circumstance"]
items: Latency, how fast a request needs to be served
Availability, how much downtime the system can tolerate
Consistency, whether every reader needs to see the same data at the same instant
Scale, how many users and requests the system needs to handle
Durability, whether data loss is acceptable under any circumstance

blocks.title: Non functional requirements are where the real design lives
blocks.content: Two systems can share the exact same functional requirements, post a tweet, follow a user, see a feed, and end up with completely different architectures once you fix the non functional numbers. A feed that tolerates a few seconds of staleness is a much easier build than one that must be instantly consistent across every region.

{"headers":["Functional (what it does)","Non Functional (how well it does it)"],"rows":[["Post a tweet","Write should complete in under 200ms"],["See a feed","Feed should load in under 500ms at the 95th percentile"],["Follow a user","The system should stay available during traffic spikes"],["Search tweets","Search results can be a few minutes stale, that is fine"]]}
4. The Core Clarifying Questions

You do not need a huge checklist of questions to run through. A small, focused set covers almost every prompt you will see, and asking these five in the first few minutes tells the interviewer you know how this conversation is supposed to start.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396383033-480327161.png
blocks.alt: Five core clarifying questions branching out from a central starting point: users and scale, read write ratio, scope, consistency, and region

blocks.content: 4.1 Who Are the Users, and Roughly How Many
blocks.text: 4.1 Who Are the Users, and Roughly How Many

blocks.content: Start with who is using this thing and at what rough order of magnitude. A system built for ten thousand internal employees looks nothing like one built for a billion consumers, even if the functional requirements are identical on paper.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396383033-826381636.png
blocks.alt: The same clarifying question, how many users, answered by three very different scale bands: 10 million, 100 million, and 1 billion daily active users

blocks.content: You don't need the exact number. You need the right order of magnitude, because that single number quietly decides whether a single relational database is fine or whether you need to talk about sharding in the next twenty minutes.
4.2 What Is the Read vs Write Ratio
blocks.text: 4.2 What Is the Read vs Write Ratio

blocks.content: Ask how often people read versus how often they write. A Twitter style feed is read heavy, most users scroll a feed far more often than they post a tweet. A logging pipeline might be write heavy, ingesting far more than anyone ever queries back out.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384084-136474913.png
blocks.alt: Writes, new tweets being posted, and reads, feeds being viewed, both feeding into a rough ratio of about one write for every hundred reads

blocks.content: This ratio directly shapes your caching strategy, your database choice, and where you spend your optimization effort. Get this wrong and you might spend the whole interview optimizing writes on a system that is overwhelmingly read traffic.
4.3 What Is Explicitly In Scope and What Is Out
blocks.text: 4.3 What Is Explicitly In Scope and What Is Out

blocks.content: Ask directly whether there are specific features the interviewer wants you to cover, and just as importantly, whether there are ones you can skip. Should you cover direct messages? Ads? Notifications? A yes or no here saves you from guessing wrong later.
If the interviewer doesn't have a strong opinion, that's a useful signal too, it usually means you are free to propose the scope yourself, which is covered in more detail later in this lesson.
4.4 What Are the Consistency Requirements

Ask whether the system needs strong consistency, where every read reflects the very latest write, or whether eventual consistency is acceptable, where reads can lag behind writes by a bit. A bank balance usually needs strong consistency. A tweet like counter usually does not.

blocks.title: Consistency is one of the highest leverage questions you can ask
blocks.content: A single answer here, strong versus eventual, often determines your entire data storage strategy for the rest of the interview. It is worth asking early rather than assuming and finding out you assumed wrong twenty minutes in.
4.5 Is This Single Region or Global
blocks.text: 4.5 Is This Single Region or Global

blocks.content: Finally, ask whether this system needs to serve one region or the whole planet. A single region system can lean on one primary database and simple replication. A global system has to deal with cross region latency, data residency rules, and much harder consistency trade offs.
5. When You Cannot Get an Answer, State an Assumption
blocks.text: 5. When You Cannot Get an Answer, State an Assumption

blocks.content: Sometimes you ask a good question and the interviewer just shrugs. "You decide" or "whatever you think is reasonable" is a common response, and plenty of candidates freeze right there, treating silence as a dead end.

It isn't. Stating an explicit assumption out loud is just as valuable as asking the question in the first place, because it demonstrates the exact same clarifying instinct without stalling the conversation.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384085-653184335.png
blocks.alt: Two paths after an interviewer says you decide: staying silent and guessing in red versus stating an explicit assumption out loud in green

blocks.content: I'll assume around 10 million daily active users, with roughly a 100 to 1 read to write ratio. I'll design around that unless you'd like me to adjust it.

Notice what that sentence does. It commits to a concrete, reasonable number. It states the ratio that will drive your caching and database decisions. And it explicitly invites correction, which means if the interviewer actually did have a number in mind, they can redirect you in five seconds instead of watching you design against the wrong assumption for the next thirty minutes.

blocks.title: Silence from the interviewer is not a trap
blocks.content: A quiet or noncommittal interviewer usually just means they trust you to make a reasonable call, not that they are hiding a hidden correct answer. Stating your assumption clearly is the expected response, not a workaround.
6. Scoping a Huge Prompt Down to a Core Slice
blocks.text: 6. Scoping a Huge Prompt Down to a Core Slice

blocks.content: You cannot design all of Twitter in forty five minutes, and trying to is the single most common way candidates run out of time with nothing finished. The skill here is picking a core slice worth actually designing, and saying out loud what you are deliberately leaving out.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384085-401858197.png
blocks.alt: A huge prompt like design Twitter being narrowed down into a core designable slice, tweet, feed, and follow, with everything else set aside

blocks.content: For a Twitter style prompt, the core slice is almost always the tweet, feed, and follow loop: posting a tweet, following a user, and generating a feed. That trio alone is enough to fill an entire interview with real, meaty design decisions, fan out on write versus fan out on read, feed ranking, storage choices for the social graph.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384086-559338606.png
blocks.alt: Features explicitly set aside from the core slice: direct messages, the ads platform, and trending topics

blocks.content: ["Direct messages, a whole separate messaging system with its own delivery guarantees","The ads platform, a targeting and auction system unrelated to the core feed logic","Trending topics, a real time aggregation problem that deserves its own discussion"]
items: Direct messages, a whole separate messaging system with its own delivery guarantees
The ads platform, a targeting and auction system unrelated to the core feed logic
Trending topics, a real time aggregation problem that deserves its own discussion

blocks.title: Cutting scope is a skill, not a cop out
blocks.content: Explicitly setting aside direct messages or ads is not you avoiding hard work. It's you demonstrating that you understand the full size of the real product and are making a deliberate, defensible choice about where to spend your limited time. Saying it out loud is what separates a scoping decision from just skipping the topic.
7. Worked Example: Clarifying a URL Shortener
blocks.text: 7. Worked Example: Clarifying a URL Shortener

blocks.content: Let's walk through what this actually sounds like in a real interview, using a URL shortener, a classic, deceptively simple prompt. The interviewer just says, design a URL shortener, like bit.ly. Here is a realistic clarification dialogue from that starting point.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384086-939422619.png
blocks.alt: The flow of a clarification dialogue: the candidate asks scope questions, the interviewer answers or defers, the candidate states assumptions, and both sides agree on a shared scope

blocks.title: A sample clarification dialogue
blocks.text:
You: Before I start designing, can I ask a few scoping questions?

Interviewer: Sure, go ahead.

You: Roughly how many URLs are we shortening per day, and how many redirects do we serve?

Interviewer: Let's say a decent sized service, you decide the exact numbers.

You: Okay, I'll assume about 100 million new URLs shortened per day, and since redirects vastly outnumber creations for a service like this, I'll assume a read to write ratio of roughly 1000 to 1.

You: Do shortened links need to expire, or do they live forever?

Interviewer: Let's say they can optionally expire.

You: Got it. And should users be able to pick a custom short code, or is it always system generated?

Interviewer: Let's support both.

You: One more. Does this need to be strongly consistent, meaning a link is redirectable the instant it's created, or is a short delay acceptable?

Interviewer: A short delay is fine.

You: Great, I'll design around eventual consistency then, which opens up some caching options I'll get into. Last thing, is this single region or global?

Interviewer: Let's keep it single region for now.

You: Perfect. So to summarize before I start: creating and redirecting short URLs, optional expiry, optional custom aliases, eventually consistent, single region, around 100 million creations a day with a heavy read skew. I'll set aside things like click analytics dashboards and spam detection for now unless you'd like me to cover them. Sound good?

Interviewer: Sounds good, go ahead.

blocks.content: Notice the shape of that exchange. Every question is short and specific. Every vague answer from the interviewer gets turned into a concrete, stated assumption instead of an awkward pause. And it ends with a one sentence recap of the agreed scope, which is what actually lets both people move into the design phase with the same picture in their heads.

{"headers":["Question asked","Assumption stated when deferred"],"rows":[["Scale of URLs created per day","100 million creations a day"],["Read vs write ratio","Roughly 1000 to 1, redirects dominate"],["Consistency requirement","Eventual consistency is acceptable"],["Region","Single region for this design"]]}
8. The Interview Angle: Small Time, Big Score
blocks.text: 8. The Interview Angle: Small Time, Big Score

blocks.content: Here is the part that surprises people: this whole phase should take three to five minutes. Not thirty. Not one minute either, where you skip it entirely and start drawing boxes. Somewhere around three to five minutes of focused, specific questions and stated assumptions.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384087-42711313.png
blocks.alt: A small three to five minute investment in clarifying questions leading to a clearer scope, a faster design phase, and fewer wrong turns later

blocks.content: And it is scored far more heavily than that short time investment would suggest. Interviewers who have watched hundreds of these conversations can tell within the first five minutes whether a candidate has done this before. Vague, unscoped questions, or worse, no questions at all, is one of the strongest early signals of a candidate who is about to struggle.

blocks.title: Good clarification sets up everything after it
blocks.content: Every later phase, the high level architecture, the data model, the deep dive into one component, is easier when it's answered against a scope you both agreed on up front. Skipping this phase doesn't save you time, it just moves the confusion later, when it's much more expensive to fix.
9. Common Mistakes

["Jumping straight into drawing boxes without asking a single clarifying question first","Asking questions that are too vague to be useful, like just asking what should I build, instead of specific ones about scale, ratio, scope, consistency, and region","Treating a noncommittal answer like you decide as a dead end instead of stating a clear assumption and moving forward","Spending fifteen or twenty minutes in this phase instead of the three to five minutes it should actually take","Trying to design the entire real world product instead of explicitly scoping down to a core, buildable slice","Never restating the agreed scope out loud, which leaves the interviewer unsure whether you're actually aligned before you start designing"]
items: Jumping straight into drawing boxes without asking a single clarifying question first
Asking questions that are too vague to be useful, like just asking what should I build, instead of specific ones about scale, ratio, scope, consistency, and region
Treating a noncommittal answer like you decide as a dead end instead of stating a clear assumption and moving forward
Spending fifteen or twenty minutes in this phase instead of the three to five minutes it should actually take
Trying to design the entire real world product instead of explicitly scoping down to a core, buildable slice
Never restating the agreed scope out loud, which leaves the interviewer unsure whether you're actually aligned before you start designing

blocks.content: 10. Key Takeaway

A vague prompt like design Twitter is not a puzzle with a hidden correct scope. It's an invitation to show how you narrow an enormous, real world problem down into something specific enough to actually design. Ask a focused set of questions about users and scale, read versus write ratio, in scope versus out of scope, consistency, and region. When you don't get an answer, state a clear assumption instead of stalling.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396384087-900844369.png
blocks.alt: The overall flow of this phase: clarify with questions, assume where needed, scope down to a core slice, then design with confidence

blocks.content: Do all of that in three to five minutes, restate the agreed scope in one sentence, and you walk into the rest of the interview solving a problem you actually understand, instead of guessing at one you never bothered to define.
